content:
Apple has asked the court hearing its lawsuit against OpenAI and other defendants to allow its hired expert to personally inspect the forensic images used in the case, while also seeking documents related to OpenAI's hardware development. Details below.

A bit of background

Earlier this July, Apple sued its former employee, OpenAI, and io Products, accusing them of stealing trade secrets.

The lawsuit involves several former Apple employees alleged to have taken confidential materials with them when they left. Apple also accuses former employee Chang Liu of coaching another Apple employee on what to review before an OpenAI interview, while Tang Tan allegedly instructed Apple job seekers to bring hardware components and other materials to their interviews.

Earlier, Apple said preliminary forensic examination showed that Liu's MacBook, used after he left the company, had run simulations during his time at OpenAI using a circuit schematic that belonged to Apple. Apple also said that data on the MacBook showed Liu had used a Mac mini, and the company has subsequently requested access as part of the case.

OpenAI later pushed back against Apple's allegations, arguing the episode was "Apple's own self-inflicted mess," claiming Apple had been too lax in its offboarding procedures and security measures, making it easier for employees to inadvertently retain access to confidential materials after leaving.

One point of contention is Apple's request to expedite the discovery process, which OpenAI opposes. Another is Apple's motion for an injunction to limit OpenAI's use of the alleged trade secrets during the litigation, which could affect OpenAI's ongoing hardware development.

Apple argues that because OpenAI is still developing its hardware products, it is necessary to expedite obtaining specific evidence, since any alleged use of Apple's trade secrets could further intertwine with that work and become increasingly difficult to untangle later.

OpenAI counters that Apple has failed to demonstrate why a separate expedited discovery process is needed, saying Apple's demands are overly broad.

With the parties at an impasse, the court ordered them to file a joint statement setting out their respective positions on expedited discovery. That document, filed last Friday, is now public.

Apple seeks forensic images and development documents

In the joint statement, Apple asks the court to allow its forensic expert to personally inspect the underlying forensic images relied on by the defendants' expert when analyzing Liu's devices, in order to determine whether Liu accessed or used Apple's confidential information after leaving.

Apple says its forensic expert has identified "material deficiencies" in the defendants' analysis and argues its expert must have direct access to the materials to determine whether other problems exist in the defendants' forensic work.

Here is Apple's statement:

Apple's forensic expert has identified several material deficiencies in the defendants' expert's analysis, including (1) the inability to locate files that were clearly used and stored on Liu's Mac Mini, and (2) the incorrect conclusion that zero-byte files or files with an empty kMDItemLastUsedDate field on the Mac Mini had not been accessed. … Allowing Apple's expert direct access to these forensic images is critical to understanding what other errors the defendants' expert may have made.

OpenAI argues Apple's expert should not be given unrestricted access to the forensic images, and instead suggests that a neutral forensic expert agreed upon by both sides handle the images under jointly agreed procedures.

Apple says this arrangement would put it at a disadvantage, since the defendants' forensic expert already has direct access to the same materials.

Beyond the forensic materials, Apple is also seeking expedited access to documents related to OpenAI's hardware development, including work on metal surface finishing, power management, and battery functionality.

OpenAI previously argued its metal surface finishing techniques were developed independently without using Apple's confidential information, and said the simulations Liu ran with Apple's confidential files had nothing to do with its upcoming products.

Apple is now seeking the underlying development records to verify these claims, while OpenAI says this is merely an attempt to "peek at a competitor."

The joint statement also addresses a number of other disputes, including:

  • Apple is further seeking forensic images from devices used by Liu, Tan, former Apple employee Yu-Ting "Alyssa" Peng, and another OpenAI employee, which contain or once contained material Apple has designated as "Apple-sourced data";
  • Records related to Liu's use of AI tools. The defendants have previously said the forensic investigation found no indication that Liu used any Apple confidential files, along with platforms such as ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, or OpenClaw;
  • Documents related to interviews for OpenAI's consumer hardware product division, including materials actually used in those interviews, and communications with employees who left Apple;
  • OpenAI claims some of the interrogatories could implicate more than 400 former Apple employees currently working at the company.

Apple is also seeking the complete LINE chat history between Liu and Peng, including technical questions Peng asked Liu about his Apple work after Liu left the company.

The defendants previously submitted excerpts of the conversations in opposing Apple's request for an injunction, but Apple argues it should be allowed to see the full conversation rather than only the portions the defendants chose to submit.
